\chapter{Si + Futuro --- What Will Happen If}
\label{ch:si-futuro}
\hlchaptermodality{197}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can put the result of a condition in the future, and keep si in the present.}

I can put the result of a condition in the future, and keep si in the present.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[si + futuro]{si + futuro}

\label{lesson:ES-C55-si-futuro}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}if I have time, I speak Spanish.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Si tengo tiempo, hablo español}.) Two presents.

Now move the second half into the future, where most real conditions actually live.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the present stays put}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{si + \emph{present}, then \emph{future}.}
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{Si tengo tiempo, hablaré español.} & If I have time, I \textbf{will} speak Spanish. \\
\emph{Si llueve, comeré en casa.} & If it rains, I \textbf{will} eat at home. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The result half moves to the future. \textbf{The \emph{si} half does not.} Spanish will not put a future tense after a \emph{si} that sets a condition — \emph{si tendré tiempo…} is simply not said.

(The other \emph{si}, the one meaning \emph{whether}, is a different word doing a different job, and it takes the future quite happily. You will meet it later.)

And you already obey that rule in English without having been taught it. Nobody says \emph{if it will rain, I won't go}. English keeps the present after \emph{if} too, and neither language explains why.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{A condition is not a prediction.}

The \emph{si} half is not claiming the thing will happen — it is setting it aside as a supposition, and a supposition has no tense to be right or wrong about. Only the \textbf{result} half makes a claim about the future, so only the result half gets the future tense.

That is why the rule feels arbitrary and is not: the two halves of the sentence are doing different jobs.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Si tengo tiempo, hablaré español}
  \item \emph{Si llueve, comeré en casa}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which half takes the future? (The \textbf{result} half, after the comma.)

And what never follows \emph{si}? (The \textbf{future tense}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
